claims.statement: [correction of C2190] From 1 Apr 2023 (Finance Act 2023), interest on listed demat NCDs lost its TDS exemption and attracts 10% TDS (20% without PAN) once interest from one issuer exceeds ₹10,000 in a financial year. This was s.193 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 up to FY2025-26. From 1 Apr 2026 it is s.393(1), Table Sl. No. 5(i), of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with rates and thresholds unchanged. The interest itself is taxed at slab rate.
claims.verifier_note: verifier evidence: The substance (10% TDS from 1 Apr 2023, slab-rate taxation of interest) is supported by AngelOne, goldenpi and indiabonds ('TDS of 10% applies ... per Section 193 ... effective April 1, 2023'). However, the present-tense 'is now subject to ... Section 193' is wrong as of 2026-09-29. Web search (2026-09-29 ~09:00 IST): saral.pro says 'With effect from 1st April 2026, old Section 193 is now remapped to new Section 393(1) Sl.5(i). Rates and thresholds remain the same.' This is corroborated by blog.tdsman.com ('TDS on Interest on Securities – Section 393(1) (Section 193)', Apr 2026) and TaxTMI. All sources are secondary.

claims.statement: [correction of C2229] Not a valid post-tax YTM. The true 20%-slab post-tax yield is below 4.6604% for an investor with no capital gains to absorb the ~₹72 premium redemption loss. The exact value cannot be computed with the permitted tools; it needs a cash-flow calculation with coupons×(1−0.20) and redemption at ₹1,000 with no tax shield.
claims.verifier_note: verifier evidence: fincalc growth.pct_change(0.05825472, 0.046604) = −0.199996, so 4.6604% is exactly pre-tax YTM×0.8. This credits a slab-rate deduction for the premium-amortisation capital loss, which Indian law does not allow against interest income. The same flaw led to C2183 being contradicted (see C2206). The claim's caveat misdescribes the problem: it is not 'no LTCG/STCG treatment on the price component' but an unallowable tax shield on the capital loss, which overstates the post-tax yield.
